name: Fair Game end-credits code (yellow-marked letters in the 2010 film's end credits)
date: film released 2010; mystery first reported to Schmeh by a reader in 2014
ciphertext_source: Cipherbrain post 36 (Schmeh 2017, sources/schmeh/posts/36-fair-game.txt), fetched 25 Sept 2026, quoting the sequence as reported by the web forum AboveTopSecret (abovetopsecret.com/forum/thread833418/pg1) from the film's own end-credits screenshots (files/2014/10/Fair-Game.png, files/2014/10/Fair-Game-2.png -- not fetched this pass). The '?' at position 4 of line 1 marks a letter Schmeh/AboveTopSecret could not read because the surname it belongs to was itself redacted in the credits for a real person's privacy (see constraints.redaction_overlap) -- this is a genuine unknown, not a placeholder to be silently filled in (rule 2).
alphabet: A-Z only, two lines of 34 characters each (line 1 has one unreadable position, so 33 known + 1 unknown)

constraints.source_film: Fair Game (2010), directed by Doug Liman, starring Naomi Watts and Sean Penn, based on the Valerie Plame affair
constraints.marking_mechanism: in the printed end credits, certain individual letters (not whole words) are highlighted in yellow; AboveTopSecret's sequence is the concatenation of those marked letters in credit-roll order
constraints.redaction_overlap: some surnames in the credits are themselves blacked out/unreadable for legal reasons (the film depicts real people); the marked letter at line 1 position 4 falls inside one such redacted surname (belonging to a person named 'Hammad' per the post), so it is unknown which letter was actually marked there -- an unresolvable gap unless a clean, unredacted print or the original credit list can be found
constraints.frequency_analysis: Schmeh publishes a letter-frequency chart of the 67 known marked letters (files/2015/07/Fair-Game-Frequencies.png, not fetched) and states 'the letter frequencies are consistent with a letter substitution' -- his own reading, not independently re-verified this pass
constraints.commenter_lead: a commenter using the pseudonym 'Martin Halpin' (itself a fictional-character name from James Joyce's Finnegans Wake -- possibly a planted or joke identity) suggested: 'don't focus on the yellow letters, better take them as markers for the following letters' -- i.e. read the letter immediately AFTER each marked one, not the marked letter itself. Schmeh notes stylistic signs (word choices like 'kaprizieren') suggesting the commenter is not a native German speaker, and flags the possibility the film's own production company is behind the comment. Untested by Schmeh as of the post.
constraints.authenticity_note: unlike several other items in this batch, there is no active forgery dispute here -- the marking is a real, photographable feature of the actual film credits; the open question is purely whether it encodes anything and if so what, not whether the artifact itself is genuine

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Test the 'Martin Halpin' hypothesis directly and cheaply: this needs the ORIGINAL, unmarked credits text (which letter in the credits directly follows each marked one) rather than just the marked-letter sequence given here -- flag as needing the film's actual credit text (names/roles), not obtainable from this spec's ciphertext alone; try first against any published full credits list (IMDb full cast & crew) cross-referenced by position. Cost $1-2, Sonnet.

2. Simple substitution anneal of the 67-68 known letters (both lines pooled, and separately) against English, judged with a matched control (synthetic English monoalphabetic-substitution ciphertext at the same N/K, same solver) -- Schmeh's own frequency-chart claim ('consistent with a letter substitution') is a lead worth testing directly rather than taking at face value. Cost $2.

3. Treat the two 34-character lines as two independent short messages (rather than one 68-character message) in case they are unrelated per-line codes (e.g. two separate initials/acrostics), and re-run test 2's judge separately per line. Cost under $1 (reuses test 2's output).
matched_control: not yet run; test 2 above specifies the design (synthetic English monoalphabetic-substitution ciphertext, same N/K, same solver)

cheap_test_done.method: Martin Halpin 'next letter' hypothesis, tested with real credit-context data already on disk: James Mulliss's comment-thread transcription (Cipherbrain post 36, comment #5/#6, 9 Feb 2023, sources/schmeh/posts/36-fair-game.txt) gives the actual credit word each of ~65 marked letters sits in. Extraction script (specs/cheap-tests/fair-game-2010/run_test1.py, credits_words.py) takes the letter immediately following each mark within its word (a documented proxy -- the next listed word's first letter -- is used for the small number of marks that are a word's last letter). Multiset check: the 65 recoverable letters match the ciphertext's 67 known letters exactly except one missing S and one missing T (2 marked occurrences the commenter's list omits) -- corroborates this is the real marking, but the transcription is incomplete by 2/67 and its list order is an UNVERIFIED proxy for the true credit-roll order (a caveat on any negative below, per rule 3's normalize-conventions lesson).
cheap_test_done.target: next-letter sequence (65 letters) judged against English: language score -2.202 (control random_p99 -1.77, real_p05 -0.944), word cover 0.462 (min 0.6) -- FAIL, tools/judge_plaintext.py verdict false
cheap_test_done.control: (a) 3 synthetic sequences built with the SAME extraction procedure on the SAME word pool, marks placed to spell a known 13-letter name (ROBERTJOHNSON, unrelated to the film): name recovered exactly in all 3/3 trials -- confirms the procedure and script are not broken and can recover a real signal when one is planted. (b) 3 random-marking false-positive trials, same word pool, same N=65: judge FAIL on all 3/3 (scores -2.134 to -2.261, word cover 0.246-0.523) -- the real target's score (-2.202, cover 0.462) sits inside this random-noise band, not below or above it.
cheap_test_done.verdict: control-backed negative for this specific realization of the Halpin hypothesis (real target indistinguishable from random-marking noise of the same design; sanity control confirms the test has power). Caveated: the source transcription is missing 2/67 known letters and its order relative to the true credit scroll is unverified, so this negative applies to THIS reconstruction, not to every possible ordering of the same words. Does not by itself close the target (tests 2-3 not run this pass, per brief).

judge.note: letters_min/max spans the redacted position (67 known + 1 unknown = 68, or 67 if that position is dropped entirely); a candidate decode should either treat the unknown position as a wildcard or be tested on the 67 known positions only

value: medium: this is one of the few items in this batch with an actual letter-frequency claim already made by the source ('consistent with a letter substitution') and a specific, testable alternative-reading hypothesis (the Halpin comment) rather than pure speculation -- both are cheap to test and neither has been tried by Schmeh or (as far as this pass's search found) anyone else
status_25_Sept_2026: open; may not be a code per UNSOLVED-SURVEY.md row 29, but this pass's read of the source found two concrete, untested leads (frequency-substitution claim, Halpin's off-by-one hypothesis) that raise this above a pure 'may not exist' assessment
schema_note: cheap_tests_in_order are proposals (rule 10: an approach is not a claim); a test actually run goes under cheap_test_done with its control. This is NOT one of CLAUDE.md rule 4's 'no ciphertext at all (film...)' cases despite being sourced from a film: unlike Untersberg's legend or the Sufi fiddle's unphotographed inscription, an actual letter sequence (AboveTopSecret's reading of the credits) is already transcribed and citable, so the first test is cryptanalytic, not a fetch/provenance check.
